subject: typewriter
pitch: A 1930s typewriter in glossy racing green. Round keys with cream letters on chrome rims in four staggered rows, a semicircle of thin type bars behind them, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller with a sheet of paper half typed, and a small brass maker's badge on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module for a typewriter model, starting with a root joint at the origin that everything else attaches to. I'm sketching rough dimensions for the body and figuring out how the base, platen, and carriage pieces should be arranged.

For materials, I'll adjust roughness and metalness on specific pieces, like a dark green matte housing and chrome-colored metal accents, using simple color strings to drive each part's look. Then I'm working out the housing shape as an extruded profile with a sloped key deck, plus laying out the key rows along that same slope.

I'm now figuring out key cap design, considering chrome rims with cream letters but worried that generating individual letter textures for 44 keys is too heavy, so I'm leaning toward a single shared texture atlas instead.

I realize I can adjust each key's circle geometry UVs to point into a cell of one shared atlas texture—an 11-column by 4-row grid where each cell holds a black disc with a cream letter, giving the glass-cap look without per-key textures.

After the rotation the circle's plane maps so its y-axis becomes -z, meaning letters read upright facing forward. I'm sizing the SVG canvas at 11 cells of 64px (704 wide) by 256 tall, likely bumping to 1024 for clarity, then drawing centered text in each cell.

Laying out four keyboard rows of ten characters each (numbers, QWERTY, ASDF, ZXCV rows) into a 640x256 grid, with monospace bold cream text centered in each 64px cell, and adding horizontal stagger offsets per row to mimic a real keyboard layout.

Now I'm working out keycap geometry on an angled deck: computing per-key horizontal offsets and per-row depth positions, then deriving the deck's tilted surface normal (about 23.6°) so each keycap's rim and top disc can be oriented correctly along that normal using a directional part placement with a specified orientation axis.

I realize the local +Z axis convention means I need to pass an explicit "up" vector of [0,0,1] for both the disc and rim so the letters face forward instead of ending up upside down. Now I'm setting up the chrome rim cylinder dimensions and positioning it slightly above the deck along the normal direction, with the top disc sitting further out along that same normal.

With the keycaps sorted, I'm moving to the type bars — thinking through a semicircular fan arrangement of thin rods arcing back from the keys toward a basket near the platen, with each bar's base positioned on a radius around a central pivot point so their tips converge toward the printing point.

I'm figuring the type bars converging toward the platen with thin chrome rods and small tip slugs, plus a semicircular basket ring swept around the bar cluster using an arc path for the chrome frame.

Now I'm laying out the platen itself as a black cylinder with knurled chrome knobs at each end, flanked by green carriage end plates sized to match the body width and platen length.

I'm positioning the carriage rail as a chrome rod running along the back below the platen, plus a thin curved chrome bail rod in front to hold the paper against the roller. Then I'm working out how the paper sheet itself feeds up from behind, wrapping around the platen so it emerges toward the front-top.

I'll have the paper follow the platen's curve from roughly -50° to 20°, then break into a straight tangent line leaning back about 20° so it stands up naturally with typed text visible on the front-facing portion.

Writing paper strip geometry...

I'll simplify: put the typed text in the upper portion of the visible paper and leave the lower part blank near the printing point, giving a "half-typed" look without worrying about exact line timing. I'm setting up an SVG viewBox sized to the visible paper length, placing monospace text lines near the top using approximate font size and y-coordinates.

Now I'm working out the hardware details—platen radius, carriage return lever geometry as a chrome swept rod with a ball tip near the left end, plus platen knobs as small black cylinders on either side, making sure their positions don't overlap with the lever's base path.

I'm also laying out the spacebar as a flat tilted box in front of the key rows, and double-checking that the key row spacing and deck slope don't cause the rim of the back row to clip into the body's front edge.

For the housing, I'm planning a brass maker's badge for the front panel—a flattened oval cylinder, possibly with an etched-looking texture for lettering, to give the typewriter a branded look.

Still working through the typewriter model...

Now I'm sketching out the body's extrusion profile, feet, spool covers, and carriage brace geometry, then working through the ribbon bar sweeps and basket support posts, platen and knob placement, and finally the curved paper mesh with its UV mapping and typed-text SVG texture — making sure orientation and winding stay consistent with the viewer's perspective before writing the final code.
